Estimators First, Installers Second

Commercial Roofers of Ontario works the stretch of the Inland Empire between Ontario International Airport and the Rancho Cucamonga industrial parks next door. Most of our week is spent on single-story roofs measured in hundreds of thousands of square feet, not the small retail patch jobs that fill a typical roofer's calendar. We approach every roof as a budget problem first and a construction problem second.

Why This Market Runs on Different Math

A leak on a strip-mall roof is a service call. A leak on a 400,000-square-foot cross-dock building near the ONT air cargo ramps can shut down a receiving door, and the roof itself represents a capital asset worth protecting on a defined schedule rather than reacting to it. Property managers and asset owners in this submarket need a number they can put in a budget line, not a verbal estimate that changes after demolition starts.

So our proposals separate membrane, insulation, tear-off, deck repair, edge metal, and drainage into individual line items with unit pricing attached to each. When something changes in the field, the change order references a pre-agreed price instead of a negotiation. That habit came from years of bidding against contractors who low-ball a lump sum and make it back later in the deck allowance.

The Buildings We See Every Week

Ontario's roof stock is dominated by tilt-up concrete warehouses with panelized wood decks from the 1970s through the 1990s, and newer steel-deck product built for Amazon, UPS, and Walmart-scale fulfillment operations. Add in the retail roofs around Ontario Mills, the event space over the convention center and Toyota Arena, and a run of airport-area hotels, and the portfolio covers nearly every low-slope roof type this trade builds.

Rancho Cucamonga's logistics parks sit close enough that owners with buildings on both sides of the city line often call us for portfolio-wide bids rather than one roof at a time. We price those the same way: building by building, with the same line-item discipline, so an asset manager can compare five roofs on one spreadsheet instead of five unrelated proposals.

What We Actually Roof

  • Distribution and cross-dock warehouse roofs from 50,000 to over 1,000,000 square feet
  • Cold storage and food-grade buildings with vapor-barrier and condensate detailing
  • Manufacturing plants with heavy rooftop mechanical and equipment curbs
  • Big-box and strip retail roofs, including pad buildings around regional malls
  • Hospitality and event-venue roofs near the airport and convention center
  • Self-storage facilities and multi-tenant flex space
  • Office and medical roofs with occupied-space phasing requirements

Reading the Climate Correctly

Ontario sits in California Title 24 climate zone 10, which means most reroof and recover scopes trigger cool-roof reflectance and emittance minimums, plus current continuous R-value targets. We build that into every estimate rather than treating it as a change order surprise once plan check flags it.

The physical climate load matters just as much as the code. Roof surface temperatures regularly clear 150 degrees in July and August, which accelerates membrane aging and pushes us toward thicker, more UV-stable systems on long-hold assets. Fall and winter bring the opposite risk: Santa Ana wind events that test edge metal and flashing, and occasional atmospheric river storms that dump real rainfall onto roofs with marginal drainage. We size gutters, scuppers, and overflow drains for both extremes rather than the average year alone.

How We Handle the Recover-or-Replace Decision

California code caps a roof at two coverings, and a lot of the older industrial stock around Ontario and neighboring Pomona already carries two or three layers of built-up and modified bitumen. Before we quote anything, we run a moisture survey. Dry insulation and sound attachment can justify a recover at roughly half the cost per square foot of a full tear-off. Wet insulation or a maxed-out layer count means replacement is the only honest answer, and we say so even when the smaller number would be the easier sale.

We model total cost over the roof's expected service life rather than only the installed price, because the cheapest bid on day one is frequently the most expensive roof over fifteen years. That lifecycle-per-square-foot number, stated plainly, is what most of our clients actually want from an estimator before they want a sales pitch.

What We Never Do

We do not promise insurance claim outcomes, invent project counts, or cite certifications we have not earned for this business. When storm damage documentation is part of the scope, we document roof conditions, photograph findings, and hand over a factual report. What an adjuster or underwriter does with it is between the owner and the carrier.

Common Questions From Property Managers and GCs

Do you bid portfolios or only single buildings?

Both. Portfolio work is common in this corridor because so many owners hold multiple buildings between Ontario, Rancho Cucamonga, and Chino. We price each roof individually so the portfolio bid is actually comparable roof to roof.

Can you work around an operating distribution floor?

Yes, and most of our jobs require it. We phase sections to what a crew can seal watertight in a single shift, keep dock doors mapped and clear, and coordinate staging with your operations team before mobilization.

How do you price hidden deck damage?

With a stated allowance and a per-unit price agreed before the contract is signed, whether that's per sheet of plywood on a panelized deck or per square foot of steel deck rust remediation. You get photos and a measured quantity, not a surprise.

Will Title 24 add cost to my project?

Usually a modest one, mostly from added insulation thickness and cool-roof-rated membrane. We show the code-required assembly and the as-is assembly side by side so the added cost is visible rather than buried.

What if my building already has two roof layers?

Then a recover is off the table under California code, and the estimate will say tear-off is required. We would rather tell you that on day one than mid-project.
